implementation_notes: CommonJS makes this trivial: `module.exports = { boot, login, sync, render, ... }` in a single `app.js` grows into the application's single mutable object graph, and because `require` caches the module every importer shares it. The Node.js module cache is therefore the god object's lifetime mechanism — one instance per resolved filename, which is also why duplicate installs produce two of them. The ES module and bundler alternatives do not fix reach by themselves, but explicit `import { invoicing }` at least makes the dependency visible in the importing file. The practical split is by module file with named exports, and the practical detector is `madge --circular` plus a search for `module.exports = {` in files over a few hundred lines.
idiom_name: one exported object literal accumulating the whole app
pitfalls: `module.exports` mutated after import is invisible: because the cache hands out the same object, callers see later mutations.
A circular require graph can leave `module.exports` half-populated at require time, which is the runtime face of the same reach problem.
Bundler tree-shaking does not remove a god object's cost — it removes the parts you were not maintaining anyway.
